tasks.title: Push the branch and read the two macOS legs
tasks.detail: 90 commits sit on `refactor/portability-and-installer` and nothing has reached `origin`. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` already runs `test` and `test-bash32` on `macos-latest` with `continue-on-error`, plus a `macos-known-failures` job that checks in the blocker list. Blockers 1-7 are cleared and each is enforced by a test; **blocker 8 is the only one left and cannot be cleared here**: the suite must pass twice in a row on a macOS runner under both `/bin/bash` 3.2 and the runner's default bash. A real bash 3.2 proves the shell floor (green on 3.2.57 via the flake, verified all night), but **BSD userland is still verified by reading, not by execution.** Push, read those two legs, then remove `continue-on-error` from both. Yours to trigger: it is the first outward-facing step in this work.
tasks.note: CI run 32474258670 at a8d1285 is green on all seven jobs, both macOS legs included -- the first green BSD userland this branch has had. That closes the blocker the workflow macos-known-failures job lists, so continue-on-error can come off both macOS legs; recorded as T37.

tasks.title: The suite is not safe to run twice at once
tasks.detail: Nine tests use the fixed path `$TMPDIR/planning-agent`, so a second concurrent run of the suite -- or one foreground test alongside a background verification -- collides over the session secret directory and fails tests that are otherwise green. It cost a full verification run tonight: 49 of 70 failed on bash 3.2 for that reason alone, and the same commit was clean when re-run with nothing else running. Either give each run its own root (a per-run `TMPDIR` prefix) or state in `run-tests.sh` that concurrent runs are unsupported, so a red result is never mistaken for a regression again.
tasks.note: b00481a gives every test its own TMPDIR at source time; 1044857 shortened it to /tmp/t.XXXXX after the deeper path broke chromium in test-mermaid-accuracy (75 chars fails, 62 passes). Not swept by run-tests.sh: a run cannot tell its own leftovers from a concurrent run live directories. The original 49-of-70 collision was never reproduced, so the class is closed rather than the specific cause explained.

tasks.title: The verification harness lives only in a scratchpad
tasks.detail: The worktree-based runner that verified every commit tonight — snapshot the working tree into a linked worktree in `TMPDIR`, run `./run-tests.sh` and `bash32-run-tests`, sweep its own leftovers, and report a leg that produced no summary as a finding — exists only under this session's scratch directory. It is the tool that caught the machine-specific `PORTABILITY.md` pollution. If it should outlive the session it needs a home in the repo, and then a decision about whether it is dev-only or belongs in the manifest.
tasks.note: 53bbf62: verify-both-shells.sh lives in the repo, MODE: DEV, registered in MAINTAINER.md and the marker gate scope. It now prints each failing test own output, which diagnosed the mermaid failure on its first run -- the old version had deleted that log.

tasks.title: Plain validation passes a plan whose instructions are all placeholders
tasks.detail: A registered placeholder is a WARN under plain validation and a FAIL only under `--complete` (`validate-plan-placeholders-lib.sh`, three paths: fail for one no author will fill, fail under complete, warn otherwise). The pattern is deliberate and documented in `validate-plan-common-lib.sh:10`. The cost showed up in a real run: "Plan validation passed: 36 work units" while all 36 steps still had `<direct action on this one target>` as their Instructions, 138 placeholders in total. SKILL.md §3.3 frames plain validation as the gate for presenting a plan as ready, and Instructions plus Acceptance criteria are exactly what an executor and a reviewer consume. The question is not whether to promote every placeholder to a failure, which would break the create-then-fill flow the WARN exists for. It is whether the summary line may say "passed" while a placeholder sits in a field nothing can act on. Options: keep the WARN but make the summary state the count and refuse the word "passed"; or promote placeholders in Instructions and Acceptance criteria only, since those two are the executor's contract, and leave narrative fields as warnings. A test would assert that a plan with a placeholder in Instructions cannot produce a summary a reader would take as ready.
tasks.note: Took the first option in the detail: the WARN stays, and the summary stops claiming readiness. A plan with registered placeholders now reads "Plan validation incomplete: N work units across M goals, K placeholder(s) still to fill in J document(s)" followed by the remedy, and "passed" is reserved for a plan with none. Exit stays 0, and the test asserts that, because promoting placeholders to errors would break the create-then-fill flow and would violate validate-plan-common-lib.sh contract 1, which says warn never counts. The count is kept by the placeholder pass itself rather than by warn, for the same reason. Reproduced first on a built plan: two work units, five placeholder warnings, and "Plan validation passed" underneath them. Verified on three platforms by CI run 32476867183 rather than locally: the local run for this commit was void, because a second verification deleted its worktree (B16).

tasks.title: The run-cache prohibition is a whole-file grep, so it cannot tell an input from a description
tasks.detail: `validate-plan-ui-lib.sh:18` builds `prohibited_pattern` from `evaluate(`, `devTools`, `inject`, `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and friends, and line 38 greps it against the entire run cache, unconditionally rather than only under `--complete`. The intent is right: a UI story must be driven by a real interaction, not by console or state manipulation. The effect is that the word `localStorage` anywhere in the file fails, including in a Starting state or evidence field where naming browser storage is the honest description of what the page does. A reporter hit this and had to reword truthful evidence to pass, which is the worst outcome for a gate: it bought compliance by making the artifact less accurate. Fix by scoping the check to the fields that describe the input rather than the whole file, which means the rule needs to know the cache's sections -- the same section-shape knowledge `document-sections.json` already holds for other documents. A test would assert that a prohibited word in an input field still fails and that the same word in a starting-state or evidence field does not.
tasks.note: Scoped to the input rather than the file. A cache_section helper takes one section of the run cache, and both the prohibition and the interaction requirement now apply to the Buffered interaction sequence, so localStorage in a Starting state or a Run result is the honest description it was always meant to be. The same defect was in the story row at line 92, which tested actions, interaction and evidence together: evidence describes the result, so it is out. document-sections.json was not needed -- the run cache has four fixed headings written by one script, so a local extractor is smaller than teaching the registry a fifth document shape. Verified on three platforms by CI run 32476867183; the local run for it was void for the same reason as T18.

tasks.title: The function files have no unit tests, only the ability to have them
tasks.detail: The T4 split put 48 functions in their own files and test-plan-libs-build.sh asserts each one is sourceable alone. That is not a test of the function. What remains is the mutation sampling that says which functions are genuinely uncovered: 24 of the 48 are named in some test file and 24 are named nowhere, but naming is a weak proxy both ways -- a function can be exercised through an entry point without being named, and a named one can appear only in a comment. Sample one function at a time. Start with the ones that have no naming test and no obvious entry-point path (plan_document_kind, plan_section_spec, plan_unknown_section, plan_render_paragraphs, plan_decode_escaped_newlines, plan_require_safe_value), since a defect there has nowhere to surface. Do not add a per-function test that only re-asserts what an integration test already proves.
tasks.note: Sampled the six named functions: five were already exercised by name in group tests since the entry was written; plan_section_spec had zero coverage and now carries per-kind mapping assertions plus the unknown-section refusal in test-lib-document.sh. Deeper sampling stays with test-plan-libs-build sourceability plus integration paths, per the entry own warning against re-asserting what integration already proves.

tasks.detail: chat/requires.tsv holds only comments, so installing chat prints nothing about the runtimes a server needs (python3 -> node -> perl -> socat, socat driving runtime/bash-handler.sh). tasks.title: Register writes go through shell helpers; jq stays the reading language
tasks.detail: Both register skills document writing as a multi-line jq program the caller pastes. That is where the damage happens: the docs already have to warn that `jq ... BUGS.json > BUGS.json` truncates the file before jq reads it, every write must remember updated_at and the skill_version stamp, and an apostrophe in a title ends the single-quoted program (it did, in this session). A verbose program copied by hand is a defect generator. Reading is the opposite case and stays as it is: the render and roll-up recipes are the flexibility the skills are for, and a wrong read costs a re-run, not a register. So: writing through helpers, reading through jq, and the SKILL.md write sections become helper calls with the jq shown only as what the helper does.
tasks.note: Asked for directly. The two child entries carry the per-skill work; this one carries the contract they share so it is decided once.

tasks.title: todo: add-task, set-status, set-field, resort and rebuild helpers
tasks.detail: Shell helpers under todo/scripts covering every write the SKILL.md documents: add a task (with parent, priority, detail, refs), change status, set a field, and re-sort the file. Each one validates the register before touching it, writes through a temp file and mv, sets updated_at, and stamps skill_version from the installed .version. Enums are checked against the schema rather than a second copy of the list. MODE: PROD, registered in skill_files() and package.json's files, and jq is already a hard requirement of this skill so no new dependency.

tasks.title: bug-report: add-bug, set-status, close and rebuild helpers
tasks.detail: The same for BUGS.json, with the fields this schema requires: adding an entry demands reproduce, observed and expected, and closing one demands a fix and a verification, so the helper refuses an incomplete close rather than leaving a fixed entry that nothing proves. Severity and priority are separate arguments because they are separate judgements. MODE: PROD, registered the same way.

tasks.title: Both helper sets refuse an invalid register and name the rebuild that repairs it
tasks.detail: A helper handed a file that is not valid JSON, or whose shape does not match the schema, refuses with a non-zero exit and a message naming the rebuild command rather than appending to a damaged file or silently rewriting it. The rebuild is itself a helper: it reads what it can from the invalid file, reports every entry it could not parse rather than dropping it quietly, and writes a register that validates. Two rules it must honour: never overwrite the damaged file in place, so the original stays for inspection the way a plan snapshot does; and never invent a field to make an entry validate, because a register that passes its own check while holding invented data is worse than one that fails it.
tasks.note: Asked for directly: the helpers instruct the caller to rebuild the cache from the invalid json using the helpers. The refusal is the interesting half -- a writer that repairs silently hides the write that broke it.

tasks.title: Test the helpers, including every refusal and the rebuild
tasks.detail: A test per skill, in the dev arm. Cover the writes (a field lands, updated_at moves, skill_version is stamped, the file still validates), the refusals each with its own exit code (unknown enum, missing required field, closing without a verification, duplicate id, absent register), text that would break a hand-written program (an apostrophe, a quote, a backslash, a pipe, a newline in a detail), and the rebuild from a register damaged three ways: invalid JSON, a valid file with a bad enum, and a truncated one. Assert the rebuild reports what it could not parse. Mutation-test every assertion: the refusals are the point, and an assertion never seen to fail is not verified.
tasks.note: The apostrophe case is not hypothetical: a jq program in this session died on `the user's` mid-string, which is exactly what a helper removes.

tasks.title: Make the plan overview a reviewing tool, not only a monitor
tasks.detail: The page answers how far along and nothing else. As a review surface it is opaque: no plan description, no goal prose, no way to open a step and read what it entails, narration truncated mid-sentence, no picture of how steps depend on each other, and no sight of the tests at all. Everything needed is already in the plan tree -- plan-description.md, goal.md, the step files and their -testing.md companions, work-unit-inventory.md with its depends-on column, the coverage table, and adversarial-review.md -- so this is a rendering gap, not a data gap. Constraints that hold for every child: one self-contained file with no external asset references (its own test asserts this), the state palette keyed on html[data-state], every interpolated value HTML-escaped through esc, and no dependency beyond what the skill already declares.
tasks.note: Asked for directly, from a render of .plans/gated-review-fix-keys: "This will be my reviewing tool, not only my monitoring tool."

tasks.title: Show what the plan is: description, goals and their outcomes
tasks.detail: Render the plan-description.md narrative sections and each goal's own prose -- the demonstrable outcome, the approach, the dependencies and handoffs -- so a reviewer learns what is being built without opening a file. Today the page names goals only as bar labels. Source: plan-description.md and each <goal>/goal.md.

tasks.title: Open a step: instructions, acceptance criteria, work unit, status
tasks.detail: Each of the 17 step-ledger rows becomes expandable, showing that step's Instructions and Acceptance criteria verbatim, the work unit it carries with its file and symbol scope, and its status with whatever recorded it. Details/summary is enough -- no framework, and it keeps the page single-file and printable. This is the single biggest transparency win: the ledger currently proves a step exists and says nothing about it.

tasks.title: Draw how the work relates: a dependency graph of steps and units
tasks.detail: The depends-on column of work-unit-inventory.md is an executable order that the page never shows. Draw it: units as nodes, depends-on as edges, goals as clusters, completion as node state, so a reviewer sees the shape of the work and where a blocked edge sits. Hand-authored SVG path data is the wrong tool at this size -- generate the layout, or render a mermaid block if the viewer can, but keep the fallback readable with no external assets.
tasks.note: The "no story on how edges touch" complaint. A graph is also the only view that makes a cycle or an orphan obvious.

tasks.title: Show the tests: which steps have companions and what they verify
tasks.detail: A reviewer cannot currently tell whether a step is tested. Render each step's -testing.md companion: the verification instructions, the browser, backend and manual sections where present, and mark steps whose goal requires testing but which have no companion. Source: <goal>/steps/<step>-testing.md and each goal's testing-requirement row.

tasks.title: Findings and review rounds, each openable
tasks.detail: The header says 7 findings and the cycles chart says none were recorded. Render the Findings table itself: each finding's id, what it objects to, its status, the work unit it is bound to and the fix claim if one exists, plus the review history rounds. For a reviewer this is the point of the page -- the adversarial review is where the judgement lives.

tasks.title: Test each new surface, and keep the single-file guarantees
tasks.detail: Extend test-plan-overview.sh per surface: the description and goal prose appear, a step expansion carries its instructions and acceptance criteria, the graph has a node per unit and an edge per depends-on, a step whose goal requires testing but has no companion is marked, findings render with their ids and statuses, and coverage rows map to units. Keep the existing guarantees asserted: no external asset references, no unsubstituted template tokens, and markup planted in plan prose comes out escaped -- the escaping test matters more once real prose reaches the page. Mutation-test every assertion.
tasks.note: Note for whoever picks this up: test-plan-overview is currently the test failing on both macOS legs (B31), so fix that first or these additions land on a red test.

tasks.title: Serve the overview live, and let the artifact stay a snapshot
tasks.detail: One renderer, two delivery modes. Served: a localhost HTTP endpoint a reviewer keeps open, updating in place without disturbing what they are reading. File: the single self-contained HTML that exists today, which is what a snapshot, a print or a published artifact needs. The two must not fork into separate renderers -- the state each mode shows has to come from one place, or they will disagree and the disagreement is what a reviewer would trust least. Feasibility is settled ground here: the chat skill already ships a portable local server as a fallback chain (python3 -> node -> perl -> socat driving a bash handler), so the mechanism exists in this repo and does not need inventing.
tasks.note: Asked for: render to a local port or artifact, both, with updating that is less jarring while reading.

tasks.title: A served mode on localhost, reusing the runtime chain chat already has
tasks.detail: render-plan-overview.sh --serve [PORT] starts a loopback server that answers the page and a JSON state endpoint, and stops cleanly. Reuse chat's runtime chain and its shape rather than writing a fifth server: python3 -> node -> perl -> socat, first present wins, refusing with 69 and naming the capability when none is there. Bind 127.0.0.1 only, and say so in the docs rather than promising more (B30 is the cautionary tale). Print the URL and the pid file the way chat-server.sh does, so a reviewer can stop it without hunting.

tasks.title: Update in place from a JSON endpoint, never a whole-page reload
tasks.detail: The page currently carries <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="15">, which throws away scroll position, every expanded section and any text selection -- unusable while reading. Served mode instead fetches a JSON state document and patches only what changed: counts, bars, ledger rows, findings. Two rules make it non-jarring rather than merely faster: never move what the reader is looking at, and never animate a value that is only being corrected. A visible, quiet marker that an update landed is worth more than a redraw -- and if a section is open, patch its contents rather than collapsing it.
tasks.note: T42j already says the figures must be right at rest; this is the other half -- they must also stay right without the page jumping.

tasks.title: The state JSON is the one source both modes render from
tasks.detail: Emit the plan's state as JSON -- goals, steps and their status, work units and their depends-on edges, findings and rounds, coverage -- and have the file mode inline it while the served mode fetches it. Then the snapshot and the live page cannot disagree, the JSON is testable on its own without parsing HTML, and anything else that wants plan state (a status line, a CI comment) reads it too. jq is already a hard requirement of the planning skill, so producing and validating JSON costs no new dependency.

tasks.title: Two reviews are the baseline: pre and final, three only when needed
tasks.detail: Implements the counting model B34 records. A reviewed plan has a pre-implementation review and a final review, so the rounds figure is 2, and 3 when a third was actually required. The depth ring counts against what the plan needs -- 2/2 complete, 3/3 when a third happened -- never 0/3, which reads as a failure against a target the plan was never meant to hit. The cycles chart plots those rounds rather than waiting for an archive file that only appears when a further round starts.
tasks.note: Paired with B34, which carries the defect and the mechanism; this is the rendering side.

tasks.title: Test both modes, and the fallbacks
tasks.detail: Served mode: the endpoint answers on loopback, the JSON validates against the state shape, a step completing changes the JSON without the HTML being re-fetched, and stop leaves no process or pid file. Fallbacks: with every runtime shimmed away the serve request refuses with 69 and names what is missing, and the file mode still renders. File mode keeps its current guarantees -- single file, no external asset references, no unsubstituted tokens, prose escaped. And the rounds figure reads 2 for a plan with a pre and a final review, 3 when a third exists. Mutation-test each: the refusals and the two-review baseline are the assertions most likely to rot.
tasks.note: test-plan-overview is the test currently failing on both macOS legs (B31), so that comes first or these land on a red test.

tasks.title: Decide what a converted test prints on success
tasks.detail: DECIDED — t_end adopted, matching the 42 tests already using it, so byte-identical stdout is not the acceptance criterion. `t_end` prints `<test>: PASS`, or `<test>: N failure(s).` and exits 1. The three T1a tests print their own success line today, so adopting the library changes their stdout. Two defensible answers: adopt `t_end` and match the 42 tests that already use it, or keep each test's existing success line and call only the finding-recording part of the library. This has to be settled before T1a, because it decides the acceptance criterion: with `t_end`, byte-identical stdout cannot be the test of a correct conversion, and the proof has to compare the *findings* instead. **Common to T1a-T1c.** Not every `exit` is a finding: a missing fixture or an absent `openssl` is a precondition and must keep exiting. Conversion changes *when* a test stops, so later assertions begin running against state a fail-fast run never reached — that can surface real failures or hit setup that assumed the abort. Prove each one the way the earlier batch of 26 was proved: capture stdout, stderr and exit code before and after, diff them, and confirm the test still fails when an assertion is broken. Counts measured by brace-matching each reporter's own body, not by an awk range: `/^(fail|note_fail)\(\)/,/^}/` runs past a one-line `fail() { …; }` into the next function and finds *its* `exit`, which is how this file came to claim 18 fail-fast tests when there are 6. 42 tests already accumulate via `t_record`/`t_fail`; 15 define no reporter at all and are out of scope here.
tasks.note: DECIDED — t_end adopted, matching the 42 tests already using it, so byte-identical stdout is not the acceptance criterion. `t_end` prints `<test>: PASS`, or `<test>: N failure(s).` and exits 1. The three T1a tests print their own success line today, so adopting the library changes their stdout. Two defensible answers: adopt `t_end` and match the 42 tests that already use it, or keep each test's existing success line and call only the finding-recording part of the library. This has to be settled before T1a, because it decides the acceptance criterion: with `t_end`, byte-identical stdout cannot be the test of a correct conversion, and the proof has to compare the *findings* instead.

tasks.title: `test-flag-coverage` cannot see a hoisted flag
tasks.detail: DONE — c38db36 took flag checks from 95 to 122; 86f5702 covered four scripts with no differential case at all. 24 scripts accept `--plan-dir` through `plan_hoist_plan_dir`, which rewrites the argument list, so the flag never appears as a literal in the script's own parser. The coverage test scans for literals, so those flags are unchecked: it cannot tell a hoisted flag from a missing one, and would not notice a script that stopped accepting `--plan-dir`. tasks.title: The sweep is documented in prose and never connected to the tool that does it
tasks.detail: A model on the older skill hit the same class five cycles running: a fix lands in one surface and not the others that mention the unit. Correction to how this was first recorded here. `SKILL.md` **does** document the sweep: "Resolving a finding" enumerates seven surfaces and calls out the coverage table and one more as worth sweeping too, and says a finding is not closed until every surface agrees. The rule is there. What is missing is the mechanism. Nothing in that passage names `plan-content.sh find <WNN> --in all`, which performs the whole sweep in one call: verified for W05 on the self-hosted fixture, five surfaces including the coverage row. So an agent reads nine surfaces to check by hand and does it by hand, which is how the coverage row gets missed twice. Two things to fix. Name the command in the "Resolving a finding" passage, next to the list it automates. And `plan-content.sh blast-radius <WNN>` has the name an agent reaches for first and answers a different question: downstream *units* by dependency, not *documents* mentioning the unit. It returns something plausible, so the agent stops there. Either rename it, or have it name the sweep in its own output. The same report describes a stale-wording guard grown to 20 phrases that caught two drifted surfaces by itself. That is a registry with a gate, which is this repo's pattern; worth asking whether the phrase list belongs here as data rather than in each agent's habits.
tasks.note: The find-command half had already landed in SKILL.md Mechanically paragraph since recording; the remaining gap was blast-radius answering a different question plausibly — it now prints a stderr pointer to the document sweep on every run. Declined for now: growing the stale-wording guard into a 20-phrase registry with a gate; the phrases live in agent habits until the drift recurs.

tasks.title: Nothing catches a unit that must edit another unit's file
tasks.detail: From the same report: W24 creates a module-level memo for a shebang predicate and exports no invalidator, while W36 in `src/sync/watcher.ts` has to drop a stale entry when a file gains or loses its shebang, so W36 can only succeed by editing `src/extraction/shebang.ts`, which is W24's file and which its own atomicity check forbids. **The fourth instance of that shape** in one plan, after the classifyShellCommand seams, the synthesis call site, and the attribution rule. That breaks the one-unit-one-target rule after decomposition, and `validate-plan.sh` does not see it. Two units naming the same file is mechanically detectable and may already be covered; a unit whose acceptance criteria require a change in another unit's file is not, and the honest first step is to find out which of the two this is. The fix that worked is a decomposition rule worth writing down: **one module over one piece of state owns every export that state needs**, so W24 took both the predicate and its invalidator, W36 depends on it, and the companion asserts that invalidation forces a re-read. That last assertion is what proves the watcher never reaches into the module. If the rule were in the atomization guidance, the shape would be caught at decomposition rather than in cycle 12. Related and not mechanically checkable: the same report found an instruction telling an implementer to reuse a predicate "whose result is already memoized", where the predicate keys on an absolute path and the callers hold relative ones. A differently spelled key is a memo miss, so the instruction cost the extra read it existed to prevent. An instruction that depends on a cache has to name the key. That belongs in the adversarial-review prompt, not in a gate. Also worth encouraging: that report deleted two units whose acceptance criteria were unreachable by construction and recorded the blocking mechanism as a non-goal. A weaker true claim beats a stronger false one.
tasks.note: Decomposition rule written into SKILL.md operating rules: one module over one piece of state owns every export that state needs; B depends on A and asserts it, never edits A file. The weaker-true-claim advice from the same report joined the no-invented-details bullet. Mechanical detection stays open-shaped (acceptance-prose analysis) and is not pretended into a gate.

tasks.title: An instruction that leans on a property must state the condition
tasks.detail: From the memo-key defect: a step told an implementer to reuse a predicate "whose result is already memoized", the predicate keys on an absolute path, and the callers hold relative ones. Every call was a miss, so the instruction cost the extra read it existed to prevent. The general rule fits an existing one rather than needing its own. SKILL.md line 73 already says to make every step self-contained and not to require the agent to infer details from unrelated files. A claimed property is the same failure in a smaller space: the instruction is self-contained in appearance only. So extend that bullet. A cache needs its key. Idempotence needs what makes a repeat safe. Ordering needs the sort key. Validation needs what was validated. Partly gateable, with care. The claim words are a short list (memoized, cached, already computed, idempotent, sorted, validated, normalised) and a step instruction using one without a qualifying clause nearby is detectable, which is the shape of the stale-wording guard in T13. The risk is crying wolf: "already validated by the caller" is a complete claim. Build the phrase list as data and make it a warning first, then decide whether it earns a failure.
tasks.note: Self-contained bullet extended: a claimed property must carry its condition (cache needs key, idempotence needs repeat-safety, ordering needs sort key, validation needs what was validated), with the memoized-predicate miss as the recorded cost. Detector deferred deliberately per the crying-wolf risk noted in the task.

tasks.title: openssl is a second runtime dependency, beyond the jq ceiling
tasks.detail: Two different uses, and only one is hard. For plain SHA-256 it is the third fallback after `sha256sum` and `shasum` (`plan-context-lib.sh`, `generate-reviewer.sh`), which is the `sha256-tool` portability rule and needs nothing. For HMAC-SHA256 it is required: `mint-fix-keys.sh` and `verify-fix-keys.sh` derive a fix key as `HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<session>|<finding>|<unit>")`, and no coreutils tool does keyed HMAC. Both guard it and exit 69 with a named message, and the tool list in `test-runtime-dependencies.sh` includes it. So the fix-key gate has a dependency the rest of the skill does not, and the recommendation here was wrong at first. Two facts settle it. The secret lives at `$TMPDIR/planning-agent/review-fix-keys/<session>/secret`, mode 600, and the reviewer and fixer run as the **same Unix user**. The fixer can read it. The gate never resisted a determined agent; it prevents accidental self-certification and makes a deliberate bypass an explicit act. That is worth having and it is a speed bump, not a security boundary. Once the threat is accident rather than attack, HMAC's advantage over `digest(secret || message)` disappears. HMAC exists to stop length extension by someone who cannot see the key, and here they can. Since this was written, two things reduced the urgency without settling it. openssl is now a declared **soft** requirement of planning (`requires.tsv` plus hints in `installer/tools.tsv`), so a host without it is warned at install time with a per-platform install command instead of discovering the gap when mint-fix-keys.sh exits 69 mid-review. And `test-sha256-fallbacks.sh` now proves the three hash branches agree, so the alternative below has a tested mechanism under it rather than an assumed one. **Preferred fix: derive the key with the SHA-256 fallback chain that already exists** (`sha256sum`, then `shasum`, then openssl) over `secret || message`. Three lines, no ipad/xpad construction, and openssl becomes one of three ways to satisfy the requirement instead of mandatory, matching every other hash in the repo. Note that `openssl rand -hex 32` already falls back to `/dev/urandom | od`, so key generation is not the problem; the HMAC call is the only place openssl is required rather than preferred. Not `cksum`, which is right for the installer's change detection and wrong here: CRC32 collisions are cheap to produce deliberately, and a fixer hand-editing `fixes.md` is the case this gate exists for. Changing the derivation invalidates keys minted by the old scheme, so it needs the same before/after proof as any migration plus a note that an in-flight review must re-mint. Smaller and separate: `test-fix-keys.sh` calls openssl with no guard, so on a host without it the run fails confusingly instead of reporting UNCONFIGURED the way `test-add-fix-claim.sh` does.
tasks.note: Unblocked by implementing the preferred fix from the entry own analysis: fix keys are SHA-256 over (secret)(session|finding|unit) through the sha256sum -> shasum -> openssl chain, identical in minter and verifier (ratchet pin updated to fix_key), openssl demoted from hard requirement to third rung with a chain-wide 69 guard, docs and both key tests moved to the new derivation. Keys minted under HMAC do not verify; re-mint.

tasks.title: A coverage row can be added and replaced, never removed
tasks.detail: `add-coverage.sh` offers add and `--replace`; the only path that drops a row is a side effect of `remove-work-unit.sh` emptying it (`plan-reconcile-lib.sh:46`, "row dropped"). So an obsolete row whose work units still exist has no sanctioned removal, and the only remaining option is the hand edit `SKILL.md:1295` forbids. Same shape as `fixes.md` having five readers and no writer, which `add-fix-claim.sh` closed. Found by a model on the older skill, which hit it while deleting units and added a `--remove` mode to `add-coverage.sh`. **Prefer a separate `remove-coverage.sh`**: this repo already spells removal that way with `remove-work-unit.sh` and `remove-plan.sh`, and a script named `add-` that deletes rows reads wrong at every call site. Whichever way, it owes the drop notice contract 9a now requires, naming each row it removes. Worth checking at the same time whether any other artifact is add-only. The question to ask of each writer is not "can I create this" but "can I undo it without hand-editing".
tasks.note: Final-gate hardening: temp files via plan_track_tmp + plan_atomic_write (no hand-rolled .tmp.$$), single awk pass captures the carried units, and the no-match status is read before the atomic write so a pipe cannot swallow it.

tasks.title: Audit this repo for a rule whose complexity exceeds what it buys
tasks.detail: From a worker report on another tree: a working-directory rebase rule bought exactly one relation out of ten, and produced roughly thirty findings across five review cycles -- the confinement set, a CDPATH predicate wrong three times, a stack-form table wrong twice in opposite directions, physical mode, stickiness, a base parameter and its unknown state. The replacement is the conservative rule that yields no edge where resolution is not obvious, costing the one measured relation. The reusable move is to measure the coverage a rule buys before deciding it is worth its failure rate. This repo has candidates: the `--stale` gate policies, the placeholder WARN/FAIL split in T18, the run-cache prohibited-word grep in T19, and the `plan_refuse_field_section` shape detection. For each: how many real defects has it caught, how many false positives has it produced, and what breaks if it is replaced with the conservative version. Precedent here is the Class A ban, approved and then withdrawn on evidence -- 24 hits, zero defects, several rewrites that made documents worse.
tasks.note: Audit walked: ratchets (duplication, function-length) demand cap-lowering ceremony but caught two real migrations today and block growth, so they pay; registry-plus-gate rules (placeholders, goal-tables, state-change, document-sections, couplings) each name their gate; the shellcheckrc silences are three documented noise checks. Closest call was cap-maintenance friction on every dedupe; kept because the alternative is caps that lie. No rule found whose complexity exceeds what it buys.

tasks.title: There is no way to renumber steps
tasks.detail: PARTLY DONE — the state is now impossible to create (f711f30) and blocks plan creation and validation loudly (10954ed). What remains is the repair path for a plan already holding one. Steps only append, and a plan that ends up with a gap or an out-of-order sequence has no helper to fix it -- the only route is the hand edit `SKILL.md:1295` forbids. A worker hit this after creating two steps numbered 04 in one goal, with no 01 or 03, and worked around it by recording an ordering note naming the real dependency edges. The duplicate-number half is fixed: `add-work-unit.sh` now refuses a step number already used in that goal, naming the file holding it. What remains is the repair path for a plan already in that state, and the answer is not obviously a renumbering helper: renaming a step file moves a path that the inventory row, the goal roster, the testing companion and any progress tracker all reference, so a rename is a five-surface edit. Options, worst last: leave it, and treat the ordering note as the sanctioned workaround since dependency edges are the real order anyway; add `renumber-step.sh` that moves one step and updates every surface, with the seven-surface sweep as its checklist; or allow gaps explicitly in the documentation so nobody feels obliged to fix them. Worth deciding rather than drifting, because the workaround the worker chose -- an ordering note -- is sound and may simply be the answer.
tasks.note: Decision: leave it. Ordering note plus recorded edges is sanctioned (already documented at both SKILL.md sites); numbering gaps are now blessed explicitly as not-a-defect, naming the five-surface rename cost that makes repair worse than the gap.

tasks.title: test-portability-contract spawns 5658 greps; invert the loop and it is one per rule
tasks.detail: Measured at 15.6s of a 164s suite, third most expensive test. It loops files-outside, rules-inside: 23 gated rules x 246 scanned files. The nesting is only that way because each file is comment-stripped with sed before grepping, so many files cannot be passed to one grep. Strip once into a temp copy per file (246 seds), then run one grep per rule over all the copies at once (23 greps): about 269 spawns instead of 5658, and attribution per rule is preserved because the rule is still the outer loop.
tasks.note: Each file is stripped once into a mirror tree, then each rule greps that tree in one pass: about 270 processes instead of 11,000. Measured 15.6s to 4.9s, so about 10s off a 164s suite. Substitution keeps the line count, so a line number in the mirror is the line number in the source. Two things the work turned up: stripping the ./ prefix from the grep output silently disabled every allowlist exemption, caught because a run then reported 28 sanctioned files; and the plan-map-lib.sh:assoc-array exemption is vestigial, since that file mentions declare -A only in a comment and comment-stripping already removes it -- recorded as T36 rather than deleted here. tasks.title: Measure inside the two most expensive tests before deciding they are inherently slow

Time the invocations inside each and separate the work the test exists to do from setup repeated per case: a fixture built once and copied is cheaper than one built per assertion. Decide per test, and record which are inherent so nobody re-opens this.
tasks.note: Measured this session under limited-run: test-plan-commands 26s, test-safeguards 18s, test-review-lifecycle 16s. Both leaders are structurally expensive: plan-commands drives ~30 real helper CLIs each paying git snapshot + interpreter startup; safeguards spends deliberate wall clock proving time-based behaviour (bounds, grace, escalation). tasks.title: The python3-shipped rule, its gate and the tree now disagree
tasks.detail: chat/runtime/server.py ships to end users, while the stated rule is that jq is the ceiling for a runtime dependency and python3 is dev-only. The gate cannot see the conflict: test-portability-contract scans *.sh only, so a shipped .py file was never in its reach, and the two allowlist entries added for chat cover the shell files that probe for python3, not the python file itself. The fallback design is intended, so one of three things should change: the rule text, so it bans requiring python3 rather than shipping it; the gate, so it can see non-shell files; or the tree.

The detector and *.sh scan are unchanged; chat/runtime/server.py remains outside the gate by construction.

tasks.title: Narration reads as an account, and is not truncated

Let it wrap and grow, and make it an actual account -- what changed since the last render, which step moved, which finding was raised or resolved, what is waiting on what -- rather than three restated counters.

tasks.title: Coverage: which outcome each work unit answers
tasks.detail: Render the definition-of-done coverage table so a reviewer can see which required outcome each unit is claimed against, and which outcomes carry no unit. The validator already refuses an uncovered outcome; showing it turns a gate into insight.

tasks.title: Make it navigable and reviewable: anchors, keyboard, print
tasks.detail: A reviewing tool gets linked and annotated: stable anchors per goal, step, unit and finding so a comment can point at one, keyboard access to every expandable, visible focus, a print stylesheet that expands everything and drops the animation, and prefers-reduced-motion honoured. The auto-refresh must not fight a reader mid-expansion -- pause it while something is open, or drop the meta refresh for a JS refresh that preserves state.
tasks.note: The 15s meta refresh currently reloads the page wholesale, which would close every expanded section a reviewer had opened.

tasks.title: Numbers must be readable at rest: no count-up animation on a review surface
tasks.detail: Every headline figure animates from zero: the donut renders 0% and counts up, the bars grow from width 0, and the narration lines fade in on a delay. On a monitor that is fine. On a review surface it is not: a screenshot or a print taken before the animation settles shows a number that is simply wrong -- a render of a 17-of-17 plan was read as 98% complete for exactly this reason, and the reader had no way to know the figure was still moving. Render the true value as the text content and let the animation be an enhancement over it, so the page is correct at rest, under print, in a screenshot, and when prefers-reduced-motion is set.
tasks.note: Found by a screenshot of the real render being read as a data inconsistency. The figures were right; the page just could not be trusted at a glance, which is the whole job of a review tool.

tasks.title: Graceful fallback, stated rung by rung
tasks.detail: Every rung has to be honest about what it gives up. With a runtime present: served, live, in-place updates. Without any runtime: the file mode, a snapshot, and no refresh at all rather than a meta refresh that reloads while being read -- a footer saying when it was generated and how to re-render beats a page that silently jumps. With JS unavailable or blocked: the file mode still renders fully, because the values are in the markup (T42j). Published as an artifact: a snapshot by necessity, since an artifact page is served from claude.ai and its CSP blocks requests to any other host, localhost included -- live updates are impossible there and the page should not pretend otherwise.
tasks.note: The artifact constraint is measured, not assumed: the current render was published by unwrapping it, and any fetch to a local port from that origin is refused by the CSP.

tasks.title: A `--check` mode for a findings CSV
tasks.detail: Validate the shape of an adversarial-review CSV without committing it, so a reviewer learns about a malformed row before it lands in the table. Was P1-5, downgraded to P2 because `update-adversarial-review.sh` refuses a malformed row anyway — the gap is that it refuses at write time, when the reviewer has already left.
tasks.note: --check runs the write-path shape gate and mint preview, prints the row count with an explicit nothing-was-written line, and exits before any table, history, key or incoming-file consumption. Pinned in test-adversarial-review-preamble.sh; mutation (dropping the exit) fails both the untouched-table and message assertions.

tasks.title: Move MAINTAINER.md's artifact map into `coupling.tsv`
tasks.detail: `blast-radius.sh` reads `coupling.tsv` to warn when one side of a coupled pair changes without the other. Some couplings still live only in MAINTAINER.md's prose artifact map, where nothing can read them — tonight's `plan_review_gated_pairs` is exactly such a pair (three scripts must agree on one parser). Each row moved turns a convention into a warning.
tasks.note: Seven prose-only couplings moved into coupling.tsv as warn rows: the three plan_review_gated_pairs callers, goal-tables.json, placeholders.json and state-change-registry.json with their pinning tests as check-commands. blast-radius stays green; MAINTAINER.md keeps the descriptive map, coupling.tsv owns the change-together rules.

tasks.title: `plan_replace_title` is a silent no-op on a colonless heading
tasks.detail: Found by unit-testing the function alone. It rewrites the title with `sub(/:.*/, ": " replacement)`, so the heading must read `# Kind: title`. Given `# NoColonHeading` it changes nothing, returns 0, and reports success. Every creator writes the `# Kind: title` form, so this is only reachable on a heading that has already been damaged -- but a rename that silently does nothing is the shape of defect the drop-notice contract exists to prevent. Either refuse a heading it cannot rewrite, or say what it did. Current behaviour is pinned in `test-lib-document.sh` so a change is deliberate.
tasks.note: Refuses instead: awk exits 3 on a heading with no colon and plan_die names the damage; the test-lib-document pin flipped from recording the no-op to asserting refusal, untouched heading, and message.

tasks.title: Decide whether MAINTAINER-STYLE-CONTRACT.md belongs in a prod install
tasks.detail: It is the one file whose name says maintainer while it still sits in the prod arm of skill_files() and is marked MODE: PROD. Shipped ROLES.md references it in prose, and four tests assert against it. Either it is a runtime contract an installed skill reads -- in which case the name is wrong -- or it is a maintainer document and should move to the dev arm.
tasks.note: Decision: keeps shipping. role-context.sh serves MAINTAINER-STYLE-CONTRACT.md to maintainer, installer, oracle and eve roles, so it is a runtime dependency of the installed gatekeeper, not a maintainer luxury. Its header now says internal means audience, not distribution.

tasks.title: Replace the codex-worker fake sleep 1 with a handshake
tasks.detail: benchmark/planning/tests/test-review-lifecycle.sh:431 — the fake worker sleeps so the runner can capture its process group for the post-run audit. That is a real synchronisation point, so the sleep is load-bearing rather than lazy, but it is still a wall clock: on a loaded runner the capture could lose the race. A handshake (the worker waits for a file the runner writes, then exits) makes it deterministic.
tasks.note: Handshake: the fake worker polls the exported BENCHMARK_PROCESS_REGISTRY for its own registration (pid match, or the worker.jsonl row if the shim forked) and exits when captured; 15s ceiling bounds a defect only. test-review-lifecycle passes.

tasks.title: launch_agent is 93 lines against the 40-line function limit, and nothing gates function length
tasks.detail: CODE-STYLE section 3 sets 40 lines per function. launch_agent was 83 before the watchdog and is 93 after. No test enforces the limit, which is why it drifted -- the same gap the deferred-refactor note records for file sizes. Either gate the limit and pay off the violations, or state the exemption for launch paths.
tasks.note: launch_agent split into _agent_resolve_isolation / _agent_timeout_binary / _agent_spawn / _agent_capture_group (all under 40, safeguards pins intact). The cap is now ratcheted by test-function-length-ratchet.sh at 67: growth fails, shrink demands a lower cap. Registered in the manifest and install.sh.

tasks.title: test-safeguards went from 0.4s to 13s; decide whether the deaf-agent case earns 6.5s of it
tasks.detail: The watchdog tests are wall-clock bound by construction: 6.5s is the TERM-ignoring agent (1s bound plus the 5s KILL grace) and 2.5s the ordinary kill case. That is the one scenario proving the KILL escalation, so dropping it removes real coverage; shortening the grace to make the test fast would weaken the production value. Options: keep it, make the grace configurable so the test can use a shorter one, or move the slow case behind an opt-in.
tasks.note: Decision: the deaf-agent case stays. It is the only pin of TERM-then-KILL escalation (an agent that traps TERM would otherwise turn the bound into a suggestion), costs roughly 5s of an 18s test (1s bound plus escalation grace plus poll granularity, measured), and its removal would trade a real guarantee for dev-only seconds.

tasks.title: The plan-map-lib.sh assoc-array exemption is vestigial
tasks.detail: in_allowlist exempts ./planning/scripts/plan-map-lib.sh from assoc-array, but that file names declare -A only in a comment, and section 4 strips comments before matching. Removing the exemption changes nothing, which is how it was found. Delete it, or keep it and say in the comment that it guards prose that no longer exists.
tasks.note: Deleted. Testing every exemption the same way found this was the only dead one: the glob entries benchmark/*, planning/tests/* and the sha256 and stat-format entries are all live, and run-tests.sh:python3-shipped needs a second look because the probe could not read glob patterns and returned an unsound answer for three of four.

tasks.title: A plan-to-HTML renderer
tasks.detail: A shell script that turns a plan's Markdown into one self-contained HTML file suitable for publishing through the artifact skill, so a reviewer can read a whole plan — description, inventory, goals, steps, findings, progress — in a browser instead of opening twenty files. Contract 15 says the documents exist to be human-followable; this is the logical next step for the reviewer who is not sitting in the repo. Constraints it must respect: no new runtime dependency (jq is the ceiling, so no pandoc/node), bash 3.2 and BSD userland, self-contained output with no external assets (the artifact CSP blocks them), and it must read plan content through the sanctioned readers rather than parsing files directly. Dev-only, so it does not need a manifest row.
tasks.note: Shipped as render-plan-overview.sh plus plan-overview.html.tmpl (5cc9e31), registered and pinned by test-plan-overview.sh (516ddc4, fe35b27); the entry was never closed.

tasks.title: Verification must surface plan-versus-reality drift at execution time, not after a human reads both sides
tasks.detail: B38: rules requiring same-turn plan mutation exist but nothing executes them, so an executor can ship code while progress reads 0% and shipped units stay out of the inventory. Candidate mechanisms, cheapest first. (a) A freshness section in validate-plan output: for each step, compare the newest commit timestamp touching its change-target paths against the step status record, and WARN when code moved after the status was set without a matching update — needs the consumer repo as --repo input, which verify-target.sh already takes. (b) An end-of-burst gate helper the executor runs before reporting: replays (a) plus inventory-vs-git path coverage, exits non-zero when any shipped path has no owning unit or any completed step whose target changed since completion. (c) The summary template may not print an outstanding list; anything it would have listed becomes either a mutation performed now or a recorded non-goal. Whichever ships, its own test drives a fixture repo whose commits move a target after completion.
